items.prompt: State what is meant by an abstract data type.
items.canonical_answer: An abstract data type is a collection of data together with a set of operations on those data, described by what the operations do rather than how the data are stored.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - data plus the operations on it, described by what the operations do, not by the storage.

items.prompt: Explain why an ADT is described by its operations rather than by its storage.
items.canonical_answer: The operations are the deal between the ADT and its user: a program that uses push and pop works against what the operations do, so the storage underneath can change without the program changing. Describing the storage instead would tie every user to one implementation, which is what the abstraction exists to prevent, because what the operations do is the only promise the user needs.
marking_guidance: Reason: the operations are the promise the user works against - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the storage can change beneath without touching any user, because the description binds the two sides only by behaviour - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 10.4 claim ledger.

items.prompt: An editor's undo list keeps each change and undoes the most recent one first. Explain which ADT this is and why its description fits the situation.
items.canonical_answer: The undo list is a stack: the changes are the data, and the operations are the push of each change and the pop of the most recent one to undo it. The stack’s rule - last in, first out, the newest leaves first - is exactly the undo rule, because the most recent change is the next one undone, so the situation matches the ADT by its leave-order.
marking_guidance: Context: this given undo list and its most-recent-first rule - 1 mark for the stack named.
Reason: because a stack’s pop takes the newest item first, which is the undo rule exactly, the situation fits the stack’s description - 1 mark.

items.prompt: State the rule by which a stack’s items leave it.
items.canonical_answer: Last in, first out: pop removes the most recently pushed item, so the newest item leaves first.

items.prompt: Explain why a keyboard buffer is designed as a queue rather than a stack.
items.canonical_answer: Keys typed must reach the program in the order they were struck, so the oldest key has to leave first - and a queue is exactly that rule, with enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front. A stack would hand the program the newest key first, so the letters of a word would arrive backwards, which is why the buffer is the first-in-first-out structure.
marking_guidance: Reason: keys must be delivered in striking order, so the oldest leaves first - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the word arrives letter by letter as typed, because the queue’s rule matches the situation’s rule, whereas the stack’s would not - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A clinic keeps a waiting list that patients join at the end and that is frequently reordered as urgent cases jump in. Explain why the list is held as a linked list rather than an array.
items.canonical_answer: The reordering is done by redirecting pointers: an urgent patient is inserted after the right node by taking over one pointer and handing one on, so nothing else in the list moves. In an array, inserting a patient in the middle means shifting every later patient one position along, so each reorder walks the whole list - the linked list edits the middle in place, which is why it suits the jumping list.
marking_guidance: Context: this given waiting list and its urgent insertions - 1 mark.
Reason: because inserting is a pointer redirect rather than a shift of later items, the frequent reordering is cheap in the chain, so the structure matches the editing - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Explain how the two pointers of a queue’s array implementation produce the first-in-first-out behaviour.
items.canonical_answer: Rear holds the index of the queue’s rear element and Front the index of its front element, so enqueue advances Rear and stores the newcomer there - the newest position, where arrivals go - while dequeue takes the element at Front and advances it - the oldest position, because Front was left behind by every earlier arrival. The two pointers walk forward one arrival at a time, so what entered first sits at Front when service comes, which is how first in, first out is produced by two integers.
marking_guidance: How the pointers work: Rear marks where arrivals go and Front where service takes from - 1 mark.
Because Front is left behind by earlier arrivals, the oldest item is always at Front, so the arrival order becomes the leaving order - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A printer holds its jobs in a queue of up to 40 jobs, each a document name. The office wants a module that works with the queue’s rules. Write pseudocode for a procedure ReportJobs that takes the array JobNames, of up to 40 strings, and the two integers Front and Rear holding the queue’s end indices, and outputs every job’s name from Front to Rear in order - the order the jobs will print.
items.canonical_answer:
```pseudocode
PROCEDURE ReportJobs(JobNames : ARRAY[1:40] OF STRING, Front : INTEGER, Rear : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Position : INTEGER
   FOR Position <- Front TO Rear
      OUTPUT JobNames[Position]
   NEXT Position
ENDPROCEDURE
```

Mark point 2: the declaration of the loop variable Position, because the module declares what it uses.

Mark point 4: the array element written by index, JobNames[Position], inside the loop. Mark point 5: the loop closed with NEXT Position.
Mark point 6: the output produced inside the loop, one job per pass, in the order they will print. Mark point 7: the module closed with ENDPROCEDURE, with no returned value.
Mark point 8: the queue’s behaviour kept - the front job is output first because Front is the loop’s start, so the report reads in first-in-first-out order, which is the whole result.

items.prompt: A switchboard holds its held calls as a stack of up to 30 caller names. Write pseudocode for a procedure UndoHolds that takes the array HeldCalls, of up to 30 strings, the integer Top holding the stack’s top index, and the integer NumToUndo, and outputs the names of the NumToUndo most recent held calls, one per line, by popping the stack’s rule - newest first.
items.canonical_answer:
```pseudocode
PROCEDURE UndoHolds(HeldCalls : ARRAY[1:30] OF STRING, Top : INTEGER, NumToUndo : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Count : INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   Current <- Top
   FOR Count <- 1 TO NumToUndo
      IF Current >= 1 THEN
         OUTPUT HeldCalls[Current]
         Current <- Current - 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Count
ENDPROCEDURE
```
marking_guidance: Mark point 1: the procedure heading with all three parameters and their types, and ENDPROCEDURE. Mark point 2: the declarations of Count and Current.
Mark point 3: the initialisation of Current to Top before the loop, so the walking starts at the stack’s top.

Mark point 4: the count-controlled loop FOR Count <- 1 TO NumToUndo, closed with NEXT Count. Mark point 5: the selection guarding each output, so a request for more holds than exist stops at the bottom.

Mark point 6: the array element output by index, HeldCalls[Current], newest first because Current starts at Top. Mark point 7: Current decremented inside the selection, so the walk descends the stack one held call per pass.
Mark point 8: the stack’s behaviour kept - the newest held call is output first, because the top index is where the walk starts - the module is complete and closed with no returned value.

```pseudocode
PROCEDURE ShowChain(BookingName : ARRAY[1:25] OF STRING, NextNode : ARRAY[1:25] OF INTEGER, Start : INTEGER)
```
